utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We continue where we stopped yesterday and that is with the examination of the witness. So can you invite the witness in? MR. MLADEN KULJANIN (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a matter that I would like to take up very briefly while we are waiting for the witness, if it would be okay with you. The various defence counsel have either filed or will very soon file some of the motions having been filed today that deal with matters that this court probably needs to resolve prior to the testimony of witnesses 15 and 16, Sabine Manke and Bart d'Hooge, who are listed as the next witnesses to be called by the prosecution. We suspect that the reason those witnesses are being called is for the prosecution to attempt to introduce the statements made by the various defendants. The various defendants have challenges of one form or another to those statements that are in the form of written motions, some recently filed, some filed some time ago. So we just wanted to bring to the court's attention that we would like to have a hearing on those matters before these witnesses are presented to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will you kindly invite the witness? (Witness enters court).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you remind him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still testifying under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Yes. We were talking about Hangar 6 inside the Celebici camp, and my further question is: approximately how many prisoners did you observe being in Hangar 6 when you first arrived in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): When I first arrived there was nobody there. The hangar was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you repeat how many people were you when you the first time get inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 60 or 70, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did this number have any variations during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The next day the next group was brought in from Hangar Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately how many people could then be there inside Hangar 6 after these people coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 100 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did this number have any further variation during your stay in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It varied daily as new groups were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you say approximately what was the maximum number of people there inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 280-300. That is in Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately in which period of time the hangar reached this maximum of people inside there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period -- within the period of 15-20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately in which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was detained on 27th May and the rest of them were coming from the late May through early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kuljanin, did you personally suffer any physical maltreatment during your stay inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did that happen once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you please describe in detail every single incident, if possible, in chronological order, starting from the first one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first one, when the International Red Cross came, that was on 12th August 1992, after they left, when the International Red Cross left, a group led by Hazim Delic burst in, about ten people, ten armed guards, and they ordered us to be beaten. Then they beat us over our backs and our kidneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you name any of these guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Kemo Mrndzic, called Bosanac, and then Camdzic. I don't recall the names of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: With what were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly kicks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many people were in the hangar at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 200, 280.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many of these people were beaten on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So how long did this beating last overall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did the people beating you say something during the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason for our being beaten was because we told the International Red Cross that we were detained there as civilians and not as members of the military. That was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was the reason stated by the people who were beating you while you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember who exactly told you something like that, if you were told directly something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not saying it to the individuals. They told it to the entire group that was in the hangar. The moment they walked in the door they started cursing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about the next incident in which you were personally maltreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion when we were taken out they had us stripped down to the waist, apparently to sunbathe, and Hazim Delic was there and he hit Dragan Kravar. Then they ordered us to re-enter the hangar, and I sat down. I could not sit down until Hazim Delic ordered it. Then he came over to me and he said: "Why did you sit down?" I said: "I'm sorry, sir. I forgot to sit down without your order." Then he said: "Turn around and raise your hands", and he kicked me four times. After the first kick I fell down. After every of his kick I fell down to the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there any other incident in which you were personally maltreated besides this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I asked guard Honda to go out to the toilet, he let me go out. When I came back, he told me to stop. Then he started hitting me. I don't know the reason for it, why he was hitting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember very approximately when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June. June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were there any other incidents in which you were maltreated besides this one personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe every single incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not count it as a beating if he would just slap me or spit on me. That was something that would happen daily not just to me but to the majority of the prisoners who were there in the hangar on the part of the guards who were guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you name some of these people who maltreated you these next occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo called Zenga, Kemo Mrndzic, Kemo Bosanac, Tundic, Padalovic. There were others but I cannot remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who did exactly Esad Landzo do to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He only hit me once, Esad Landzo that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe this occasion in detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came outside. When I was returning back he kicked me. I don't know the reason for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Returning back from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: With which -- with what did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He kicked me with his boot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you have any other incidents in which you suffered personal maltreatment you have to talk to us besides the one you already described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not beaten, but I was mistreated. On one occasion I was called to Pavo Mucic's office and Delic was in there as well. I walked in there and they asked me a question. There was a bullet from some weapons, I don't know which one. Then I was asked: "What is this?" I said: "I don't know what it is. I cannot recall what it is." Then they asked me whether I made love to any Bosnian or Muslim woman or Croat woman and I said "No".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who asked you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic and Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the command building within the camp compound, in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately when did that happen? At least in which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who brought you there to the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. One of the guards. I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did this concern you alone or any other prisoners? I mean, were you brought there alone or with some other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion I was brought in alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Now, your Honour, my next question will deal with some protected witness, so I would ask you to proceed in private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let them get into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Right. Now, Mr. Kuljanin, did you personally eyewitness any other mistreatment of any other prisoner while you were in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Would you please describe in detail every single incident you may remember that you personally saw one by one. Please do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Landzo, Zenga, Esad Landzo, known as Zenga, entered the hangar and called Vukasin Mrkajic, told him to take his clothes off. He only had his pants on, his underwear. Then he put a fuse to him and set light to it, and he ordered him to run round between the rows where we were sitting. He ran screaming. He didn't dare to stop the burning fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did that happen, at least the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Again, do you remember from which position you could eyewitness this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be seen regardless of where you were sitting, but I was sitting in position number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Then did you see other incidents concerning other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dusko Bendjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo, known as Zenga, brought a small bottle -- I don't know what was inside -- and he poured the liquid over his legs and set light to it. After that he had enormous burns and blisters and this lasts for a long time. He was given no treatment and then it festered, the wounds, and it couldn't heal. When he put on his trousers, the trousers stuck to the wound and whenever he tried to release the trousers, the wound spread, and he was sitting very close to me, so I could see all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Then can you say approximately when did that happen, at least the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June, July, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe the next incident you might have seen with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same way Nedeljko Draganic was treated. The same happened to Nedeljko Draganic. Esad Landzo walked in with the small bottle. He poured the liquid on his legs and set light to it. Nedjo Draganic was sitting opposite from me. When he set light to this, he didn't dare extinguish it and then there were enormous burns. There was no medical treatment. Not one of the doctors came to see what had happened to Nedjo, to Dusko and a third man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Again can you remember approximately when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was mostly in June and July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: From which position could you eyewitness this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Position number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is there any other incident of maltreatment of prisoners you could eyewitness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirko Dordic, Mirko Dordic. He was called out by Esad Landzo, known as Zenga. Mirko got up. Esad Landzo was standing at the entrance. He had a knife in his hand. Then he heated the knife and ordered Mirko to stick out his tongue and he put this heated knife to his tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Again, do you remember approximately when did that happen, at least the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June, July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And the position from which you could eyewitness --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Any other incident you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Momir Kuljanin. Zenga also heated this knife and ordered him to put out both the palms of his hands. Then he used the heated knife on his palms. Enormous blisters developed on Momir's palms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did that happen, at least the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: From which position you could eyewitness this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1, position number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is there any other incident suffered by other prisoners you might remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The translation doesn't come.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Samoukovic Bosko was about 60. Esad Landzo entered the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened then after Esad Landzo entered the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked Bosko, whose name he had called, what his surname was. He told him "Samoukovic". He ordered him to repeat it out loud, but one could easily understand what he had said. We had all heard him. He said that his name was Samoukovic. Then he hit him once while he was sitting. Then he took him towards the door. He took a plank. It was about 5 cms thick, about 1 metre long. Near the door he hit him. Bosko fell and he didn't get up again. Several prisoners took him away somewhere. I don't know where they took him. After that we heard that Bosko had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to what he heard and ask that that be stricken. That is hearsay and that is not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to the Rules of our Tribunal an absolute exclusion of any hearsay evidence -- an exclusion for a matter of principle of any hearsay evidence does not belong to our legal system. There is a matter of reliability, of non-reliability of hearsay evidence. The reliability has to be assessed, can be assessed case by case by the Chamber. This is the Tadic case law on hearsay. In this case we have an information given to our witness in a way which I cannot see how it could be unreliable. Anyway, the main point is that a general exclusion for a general principle -- for a general matter of principle of hearsay evidence does not belong to our legal system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he can be asked from where did he hear this, from whom did he hear this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I can do that, if you wish. Mr. Kuljanin, from whom did you hear that Bosko Samoukovic died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it from his sons, Milan and Necko, who were with me in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am sorry to intervene. Can I remind your Honours of the decision in the Tadic case. It is paragraph 19 of that decision. The prosecution has in my submission according to that decision, and I can hand your Honour the copy that I have if you want to refresh your memories of this. It says this: "Accordingly, in deciding whether or not hearsay evidence that has been objected to will be excluded, the Trial Chamber will determine whether the proffered evidence is relevant and has probative value focussing on its reliability. In doing so, the Trial Chamber will hear both the circumstances under which the evidence arose as well as the content of the statement. The Trial Chamber may be guided by, but not bound to, hearsay exceptions generally recognised by some national legal systems as well as the truthfulness, voluntariness and trustworthiness of the evidence as appropriate." Your Honour, what the prosecution has to do is lay a proper foundation for adducing the circumstances in which the evidence or the statement of the person not before the court was made. Simply to say who made it is not a proper foundation, in my submission. It has to go much further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the foundation has been made further by all the facts relative to the man being beaten, taken out, and then he later being heard to have done it. Those are all factors earlier to his death. That is the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In my submission, your Honour, it has to be this, if I may suggest this. How soon after the incident did it take place? What time of day? What was the demeanour of the person who was saying it? Were they distraught? So on and so forth. Those are the circumstances that determine the reliability of the person who is making the statement. That is what the Tadic Decision is aimed at, in my submission, and it is that foundation that the prosecution has to lay in every case where it seeks to rely upon hearsay. That is my submission. I respectfully suggest that my learned friend has not laid that proper foundation and should not be allowed to adduce that evidence, unless he can do so with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think it is as absolute as that. I think much of the foundation may be acceptable if it is relevant and I think it is relevant. The only answer is the probative value might be less than what you say. Definitely the evidence is relevant to the death of the person he is indicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to join in the remarks of my learned colleague, Mr. Greaves, and also point out that the way this answer has solicited was without any prior identification of the speaker or any other information about the circumstances under which the statement was made. Now there cannot be under those circumstances any foundation having been established by anyone. Under the Tadic Decision the burden to prove reliability is upon the Prosecutor, and to simply ask a question: "What did you hear about what happened?", gives this court no basis upon which to make a Ruling regarding whether or not that hearsay might be reliable and admissible. That is the problem with the way the question was put. The question should be put in a way that first identifies the time in relation to the incident, the identity of the speaker, the relationship of the speaker to the various parties involved, so that this court can have some basis upon which to make a decision regarding reliability, but I submit that the court cannot make that decision on no basis or upon some presumption that, because there has been prior evidence regarding an incident, that that somehow makes a speaker reliable. I do not think that that follows. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I give an answer to this argument, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I would say that when any piece of hearsay evidence comes out from the account a witness is giving in open court, this is exactly the way hearsay evidence is likely to enter into the understanding of everybody in the court room. So the assessment of unreliability has necessarily to be done immediately inside the testimony itself of the witness who is bringing out this hearsay information. So again I quote the Tadic Decision on hearsay, which fixes some parameters: truthfulness, voluntariness, trustworthiness, through which a frontier can be drawn immediately between reliability and non-reliability in the immediate moment of a testimony like this is coming to the court. In a case like this the assessment of this prima facie reliability issue has to be done immediately, case by case, on a case by case basis by the Trial Chamber, because the general rule is that a general exclusion for a matter of principle of hearsay evidence does not belong to our legal system. Again, I would say we have to distinguish between this prima facie assessment of reliability and the further assessment on the probative value and on the weight to be given to this evidence. This is another problem which has to be assessed later on. In this case we have a witness who gives information in a clear way, precisely, identifying the persons and the circumstances in a way immediately after the concerned event without any motive to fabricate. So I would say that reliability, scrutiny, is enough in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, first I would like to join my learned colleagues' position. I just point something out. My friend on the prosecution seems, I think, to be turning it on its head. The Rules here do not recognise hearsay. They recognise all evidence be treated the same way, which is: is it probative? Is it relevant? Is it reliable? If, for instance, I were to say: "I want to introduce this picture or this document", and not show why it is probative, why it is reliable, why it is relevant, especially reliable prior to the time it was admitted, my learned friend would surely be objecting, because I have to show its admissibility prior to the time I ask to have it admitted. Secondly, there are two different concepts I think that the prosecution is confusing or mixing. One is the concept of admissibility and the second is the concept to be given to weight -- weight to be given to evidence once it is admitted. You have -- may have very, very probative, very, very good evidence, which should be given great weight, yet it may be excluded for some other reason. It may have been gathered in violation of international humanitarian law and be excluded under the rules. So the court would not even have to consider how much weight to give it. Before we consider the weight to be given to evidence, it has to be admissible. With those remarks, your Honour, I join with what my friends have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that where we find ourselves at this point is that the Prosecutor and I are largely in agreement regarding the law in this regard,. Where we diverge is the prosecution seems to want to do this in a kind of backwards order: first, solicit the hearsay and then establish the foundation which supports its admission. That is the backward way to do it. The prosecution controls the order of its presentation. The prosecution has had an opportunity to prepare its witness. The prosecution knows the nature of the testimony the witness is about to give when it puts the question. It is the order of the issue that is important, and that is the prosecution must lay the foundation first before the hearsay is elicited. That's the problem, as I see it, at this point. I think we agree on what the law is pretty much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, do you still have anything to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have two things I want to remind your Honours of, if I may, please. It is paragraphs 15 and 16 of the principle majority Decision in the Tadic case. That says this: "The Trial Chamber is bound by the Rules, which implicitly require that reliability be a component of admissibility, that is if evidence offered is unreliable, it certainly would not have probative value and would be excluded under subrule (89)(c). Therefore, even without a specific Rule precluding the admission of hearsay, the Trial Chamber may exclude evidence that lacks probative value because it is unreliable. Thus the focus in determining whether evidence is probative within the meaning of subrule (89)(c) should be at a minimum that the evidence is reliable. 16. In evaluating the probative value of hearsay evidence the Trial Chamber is compelled to pay special attention to the indicia of its reliability. In reaching this determination the Trial Chamber may consider whether the statement is voluntary, truthful and trustworthy as appropriate." That is the majority decision, your Honours. The learned judge, Judge Stephen, said this as well in dealing with subrule (c): "Much will depend upon the context and character of the evidence in question." I say again the Decision in Tadic says this: The prosecution, before it can adduce words that are said by a person who is not in court, must lay the foundation for that evidence in order to demonstrate that it is reliable. If it cannot do so, it may not be allowed to adduce the evidence. In my submission, the prosecution have throughout this case not done that exercise, and we have served a notice saying that on every occasion when they cannot lay the foundation we will get up and object to it. This is what we are doing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Am I allowed, your Honour, to add something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before you do that, I would like to know: are you examining Samoukovic's son as a witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you examining the dead person's son as a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No, your Honour. Anyway I would add that, since a hearsay like this obviously comes out suddenly during the testimony, this assessment cannot be done except in this very moment, as we are doing, but I would say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is a fairly difficult thing to say. You cannot do it. The issue is: how reliable is the evidence of this witness, who is telling you what someone else has told him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Well, in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is the main thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In this case I would say the solution is even rather easy, because we are talking about a person who the witness said: "I heard from somebody else that died." I will point out that we start our trial on March 10th. We had a number of witnesses and this issue of Bosko Samoukovic being actually dead is rather unquestionable. Since the hearsay evidence we heard today is simply about the fact that Bosko Samoukovic died, I cannot see how we cannot consider reliable this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is a little awkward. You mean, because we have been hearing that other witnesses have said he died, that is sufficient evidence of reliability of that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This -- the fact itself of the death of Bosko Samoukovic comes out from other circumstances we had the chance to hear in this trial in the previous hearings. So I think this is part of our set of information, and I think this can be used by the Chamber to assess concretely the reliability of the information about Bosko Samoukovic being dead. This is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Who saw him dead? Who saw him dead?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We had other testimonies, previous testimonies, through which the death of Bosko Samoukovic was explained as a fact being actually occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What you are saying here -- you are now relying on his children telling their fellow inmate that their father had died. How reliable is their own information that their father had died?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am relying about the Tadic case law. Reliability cannot be excluded in an absolute way. In my opinion the reliability in this case is unquestionable considering the parameters set by the Tadic case law. What we said is reasonably credible. The information was given to him by persons inside the camp in the immediate time in a rather precise way. So this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How were they associated with his death? Do they know where he died?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I am entitled to ask any other questions about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No, because they were all together with him in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Those two children were together with this witness in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And were not at the place where their father was alleged to have died. What was their own information? How could they have sworn to the fact that he had died?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In my opinion this applies to the real probative value of this information and the weight of this evidence. Personally I believe that this is not very important evidence which has come out now about the witness having heard by somebody else that Bosko Samoukovic has died. I do not believe that this is a very important information, even for our prosecution case, but it came out and it happened already in the past hearings that some witness said: "This was told to me by so and so." No discussion like this arose until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The fact having been presented as it has arisen now, if at any stage anybody came up to give evidence that somebody told him somebody had died, that would not be evidence of the death of that other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am not saying that that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is what you are trying to do here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are linking up the death with the beating. The death has occurred but whether it was as a result of beating or not is a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am not claiming that we have to reach a conclusion on the link between the beatings and the death of Bosko Samoukovic on the basis of what we are hearing today. My submission is that all this and all the other evidence on any other count will be the result of the entire set of testimonies and evidence which will be carried on during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We have been hearing a lot of people who died. I think that might not even matter. People who might have died, whether they are relevant or not, that is another thing, when you come forward to give evidence positively about the death of a person, which means we should now accept it as a fact that that person died, as a result of a beating; this is the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If that is what you are pursuing, it might be difficult to link this with the evidence this witness has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My submission is that this witness is not in a position to say anything more than he said on this incident. I am not claiming, pretending this witness to have -- can give us anything more about this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Then you do not have to pursue it, which means the objection is valid. He cannot go further than to say he knew he was taken out and that was the end of it, and not what his children told him, who were not in a position to give that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. We can pass to another issue in that case, but still I think I have to put my answers to the witness in order to have -- my questions to the witness in order to have answers to the extent he is informed. If he only saw some beatings and does not know what happened later on, and simply said what he heard about what might have happened later on, this is enough for me. I am trying to get from this witness only what he eyewitnessed, only what he saw with his eyes. This is what I was doing actually until this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought the defence has raised the objection because you were linking up the death of Bosko with the beating given to him by Zenga and that is why they stood up. How do they now how he died? Maybe the son knows his father is dead but that does not necessarily link it with the beating given to him by Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only asked this witness to tell us what he saw with his eyes about the incident concerning Bosko Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He did not see the death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He did not see the death, but I did not ask him anything about the death of Bosko Samoukovic. I just asked him to say what he saw as incidents concerning any other prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We have spent too long on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I offer something of assistance to my learned friend. I am not trying to be difficult or anything. I am just trying to apply the law. I have the advantage over all of my learned friends in this court in that in England an Wales counsel both prosecutes and defends. If I was in his position as soon as there is any sign of a witness being about to tell us something he has heard, conventional hearsay, it would be right to stop the witness and say: "Before you tell us what is said, give us the circumstances in which you heard the conversation." Then, if he has then established and laid the foundation of proving its reliability -- and in this case the burden of proof lies upon him -- then he may go on to ask, with your Honour's leave: "Tell us what was said", but only if the essence of reliability has been proved. That is point one. The second point is this: I notice the phrase "this evidence is reasonably credible" creeping in. The standard of proof in this court is "beyond reasonable doubt". "Reasonably credible" is not good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is not the stage when we talk about the higher burden but definitely it comes at all stages. When the prosecution is proving any point, it has to prove it beyond reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Of course I have to prove it beyond reasonable doubt, but case by case and testimony by testimony. I cannot prove any single account. I can only get out from any single witness what the single witness can know. Anyway, in future I will do what my learned colleague has suggested to do and I thank him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually he was being helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And I thank him very much. Otherwise we do not have to do with a jury in this trial but with professional judges. So if anything comes out which is not exactly what would be deemed proper for a jury, I do not think we should worry so much, since we are in a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is a matter to worry about, because it is fundamental.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let us say now: Do you know any direct knowledge about the circumstances of the death of any prisoner inside the camp? I mean, did you directly eyewitness some incident which was concluded with the death of a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zjelko Cecez called Spanac was called out at 1 o'clock, after midnight, by a guard. He was taken out in front of the hangar. I did not see who beat him, but I heard his moans as he was moaning in front of the hangar. After he was beaten four people were called out from the hangar to carry him back in. It was night and in the morning, when I woke up, Zjelko Spanac was lying dead two metres away from me. He remained in that position for two days. That is the proof. That is the proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you eyewitness any other incident which was concluded with the death of a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zjelko. The death of Zjelko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Zjelko whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zjelko Klimenta.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you eyewitness this killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emir Kovacic walked in the hangar one day and brought to Zjelko a pack of cigarettes. He was followed by Hazim Delic, who said: "Why are you giving it to him? Fuck him! He is not going to need it." I apologise for this expression, but those are the words of Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next day early in the morning Zjelko Klimenta was taken out and together with him Garo Kujundzic also went out. I don't know his first name but his given name was Garo. A shot was heard and Garo returned to the hangar. We asked him: "Garo, what happened?" He said that Klimenta was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again we are back to an out-of-court statement. We have asked him what happened and here is what he said without the foundation having been laid. We just went through that. I am not going to repeat all that argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You know, your Honour, in our opinion foundation exists already and is clear from what the witness is saying. This is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: There is a direct link.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Again, in this case we have an information given to the witness in a clear, precise way by a precisely identified person, and immediately after the concerned event without any motive of fabrication. So this first glance reliability can be assessed in a positive way immediately. Otherwise we should reach the conclusion that any hearsay is anyway excluded for a matter of principle in our legal system, which is not true, because the case law in the Tadic case and the previous Decisions of this Chamber is not -- were not in this direction. In this case we have a person who came back and told him immediately something. If this has to be excluded from the transcript, I would object to that, but I cannot say anything else than at least in this case foundation exists already, and it is clear from what the witness is just saying right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you asked him whether that was the last he saw of the person?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My question was to say what he saw about this incident, totally or partially saw about this incident, and this is the account the witness is giving to us. This is part of this witness's account on the incident concerning Mr. Zjelko Klimenta. So I ask your Honours to allow the witness to go ahead in his account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am asking: have you asked him any further questions after he had seen -- after he got the information whether he --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He was right saying to us and he was interrupted by the learned colleague of the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He had completed saying what he was telling you. He has given his answers. Did you further ask whether he had seen the man after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean Zeljko Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Did you see Zeljko Klimenta after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you tell us the detail of what you saw about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went to the toilet Zjelko Klimenta was lying near the hangar, dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This concludes your account on this incident, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is there any other incident you could eyewitness which was concluded with the death of a person inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milorad Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Again can you say what you exactly saw with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Macic, whose nickname was Makaron, walked in and it was the Bairaim Muslim holiday and he said that he would kill a number of us. However, he called out Milorad Kuljanin. He took him out and one shot was heard being fired. Following that, after that was finished, I also went out and Milorad was lying in the same place where Keljo had been lying and he was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Was any relative of yours detained also in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my father, my brother, myself and a number of my relatives, friends and kin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is the name of your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milenko Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you see your brother while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the beginning but later yes, because he was in Hangar Number 9 at the beginning. Later he was transferred to Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Later when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in September he was transferred to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, did you know any of the Celebici guards from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Esad Landzo by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What role did you observe Delic having in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How frequently did you see him inside Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any chance to talk to him besides the time when you were in the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there a time when Mr. Delic had some problem with his legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but that did not impede him to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not responsive. He was asked if he had any problem with his legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My question was which kind of a problem did he have at his legs. Do you remember which problem? How could you guess that he had a problem at his leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he had plaster in the beginning. I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what his problem may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tall, rather widely built, receding hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the court would look at the monitors, just a second ago, while he was being asked to describe Mr. Delic, Mr. Delic's face popped up on the video monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it your case that he did not know Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. My position is when you are asked to describe a witness, the TV people should not put his face directly in front of the witness while he is doing the describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Maybe the video of the witness is not on? The video is not on, I believe. It is on?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, it is not. It is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We always check beforehand that the video of the witness is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is not a point in argument, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. It is just I wish that somebody would instruct the television people when someone is being asked to describe a witness, let us not put it on television. It makes for an awfully easy identification if an issue of that does pop up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He must have seen the face so many times he can recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In any case, your Honour, the video of the witness is not on. So can you describe Mr. Delic again? You were describing him. You were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic: height, 180-185 cms, rather broad, strong, receding hair, brown hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo: height, 175, thin -- he was at that time -- brown hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What role did you observe -- I mean, did you have personal knowledge of who was the commander of the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you see him in the camp besides the occasion you already described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many times approximately did you see Mr. Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him inside the camp on about two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Two occasions besides the one you already described or including the one you already described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Please, we have got to get -- which question is he answering and what answer is he giving to which question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That is my interest too. I want to know how many times did you see Mr. Mucic in the camp besides the occasion you already described in the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him twice inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Twice inside the camp. So can you describe these two occasions when you saw Mr. Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say when was the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In August, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean August or September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where in the camp did you see him in this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the camp, inside Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you give us some details about this visit of Mr. Mucic inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion he and Delic walked in. They had a list of people with them, and they started reading it out. They were going to move them to the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Then let us go now to the second occasion you saw Mr. Mucic in the camp. Can you give us some details about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The second time I saw him when he called out Bato Kuljanin from Donje Selo. He called him out, to come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean out of Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic in any of the occasions you saw him wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In every occasion or only in some occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On all occasions when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever have a chance to talk to him besides the occasion you saw him in the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Mucic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where did you see him before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember: when did you see him the last time before your arrival at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kuljanin, were you ever interrogated by military investigators during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you give us some detail about this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me where I lived, what I did and whether I had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say "at the beginning", can you approximately give us a date or anyway a period of time when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In June, early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where inside the camp were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you interrogated by one person or more persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two, two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of these two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stenek. I don't know his first name, but Stenek. The last name is Stenek.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the other person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you accused of anything specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did they have some insignia on their uniforms as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you sign any piece of paper after this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall, but even if I did, I had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was that a long interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember what did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did they ask you during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me whether I had weapons, where I was, what did I do, who was the person in charge of Bradina, who armed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were there any judicial proceedings against us after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anybody take your valuables on the occasion of your arrest or during your detention at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That happened immediately upon arrival in the Celebici camp on 27th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What valuables did you have to hand over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we had gold, money, documents and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever get your property back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did you leave Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17th November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened to you when you left Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was transferred to the sports hall, Musala in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know who was the Commander of the Musala camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ismet Habibovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Mucic inside the Musala camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is not charged with any offence in relation to Musala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has not seen him, he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It has to satisfy the test of relevance, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said "no".

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do apologise. I am leaping to my feet too soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, we have to break for 30 minutes. We will come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please invite the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind him he is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that you are still testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. So, Mr. Kuljanin, when were you released from any kind of detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 6th October 1994 I was exchanged in Sarajevo in the presence of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. I believe this ends my examination-in-chief, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How have you decided to go about cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will proceed in this way: first, counsel for Mr. Delic; second, counsel for Mr. Mucic; third, counsel for Mr. Delalic; and, fourth, counsel for Mr. Landzo

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Moran. You may take the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran and I represent Hazim Delic in this case. I'm going to ask you a few questions. Basically I'm just going to go over your statement. It may be one or two things that you didn't talk about on direct that I may ask you about, but basically I'm going to go down my notes of what you testified to on direct examination. Now most of my questions will probably require a "yes" or "no" answer. If you can answer it with a "yes" or "no", will you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sometimes, like all lawyers, I get tongue-tied and my questions may be a little complicated or you may not understand them, and if you don't understand one of my questions, will you stop me and I will clarify it and work with you so that you understand it. Can you do that for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You were born in Konjic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: On June 15th, 1971?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You lived in Bradina basically your whole life; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You were registered to vote in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of a voters' list in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You were registered to vote in the Konjic municipality, though; is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What vote are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just in general you were eligible to vote in elections in Konjic, were you not? Let me give you an example. You could have -- I am not asking whether you did vote and I am not asking how you voted, if you did, because that is your business and nobody else's, but there was a referendum in March 1992. Do you remember that referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You could have voted in it if you wanted to, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I recall, and stop me if I am wrong, because I am going through my notes trying to find it, you testified you were not a member of any kind of a military unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, one of the things that you told the International Committee for the Red Cross was that you were a civilian, not a prisoner of war; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When the city of Bradina came under attack, the village, that lasted, what, two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And was there any defence put on by the people that resided in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So basically the attack was for two days. There was shelling and nobody tried to enter the village; is that what you are telling the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village was big. They entered one of the hamlets on the first day. It's called Suljina Strana, a hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But nobody attempted to defend the village in any way, and yet it took the soldiers from the HVO and the TO two days to take this village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you were first arrested, that was on 27th May 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There were a bunch of people there, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Imprisoned people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, people when you were arrested, at the scene of your arrest in Bradina, when you were taken to the Mico restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a group of people, about 50 people, who were captured in front of the Mico cafe. I joined that group later and they were from my neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about set to mention a name and my notes are not clear on whether that name is a protected name or not. Can we go into private session for long enough to say that name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Since we are in doubt, you had better get into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. When in doubt, I would rather ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we get into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not going to mention the name again. I may refer to him as that person, but the name is not going to come out again. When you were initially arrested and initially captured the soldiers from the TO and the HVO beat everybody pretty severely, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, there was a stop, was there not, in a tunnel or some place on your way between Bradina and Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. By the way, "I don't remember" is a fair answer if you don't remember. Let me ask you about some of the conditions in Hangar 6. Do you remember when you got there a situation where some people had blankets and some people didn't have blankets? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that at the moment when we arrived in the hangar nobody had a blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But didn't some people get access to blankets shortly afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you do not remember an incident where Mr. Delic had the blankets cut up so as many people as possible could get some part of a blanket? You don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me jump ahead a second to the food conditions. Do you know whether the food was cooked inside the camp or whether it was brought in by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether your rations were any different from that that the guards had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have rations. We had just one ration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Do you know whether what you ate was anything different from what the guards ate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But you do not know; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I do. If the guards got what we got, then they really fed well, because we didn't get food. It wasn't food. These were scraps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me jump forward to the meeting on August 12th 1992 with the International Committee of the Red Cross. You remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you talked to the representatives of the Red Cross what guards were in Hangar 6 with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not one of the guards could be present, because the Red Cross didn't want the guards to be present when they spoke to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. After the ICRC, the Red Cross representatives left, I believe you testified that everybody in Hangar 6 was beaten; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, there was a group of ten guards that came in and beat and kicked, what, 200 -- and there were about 200-280 prisoners in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it lasted an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How long were you beaten in that incident? 15, 20 minutes, 5 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let me jump forward to the death of Zjelko Klimenta; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I recall your testimony here, and stop me if I am wrong, you said he was taken out of the hangar and you said: "A shot was heard and Garo returned to the hangar and said he was killed." Is that what you testified to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You didn't hear that shot, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: On February 21st 1996 did you give a statement to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You gave a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That statement was read to you in Serbian, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it was true and correct, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably it was true. It need not mean that everything could be there. I couldn't recall everything at the time I was making that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure, and if you didn't recall something and it was left out, that is one thing, but what you said in that statement was true, was it not? What was written down there was all true, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, you signed -- the statement you signed said that the statement is true to the best of your knowledge and recollection and that you were aware that it may be used in a legal proceeding before this Tribunal. You remember that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't remember everything at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure, and I'm not saying that you did, but do you remember saying in that statement: "I believe ..." -- having to do with Zjelko Klimenta's murder: "I believe he was shot dead but today I cannot say for sure that I heard any shot after Klimenta was taken out"? Do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If I let you see a copy of your statement translated into Serbian, would that refresh your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If I showed you a copy in English with your signature on it, would that at least refresh your memory as to the statement itself? Sir, would it be helpful to you if I showed you your statement either in Serbian or in English to recall making it and maybe refresh your memory about what it said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It would help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the usher could just show these to him. (Handed). One is a clean copy in English with his signature on it and the other is a translation I believe that was done by the Office of the Prosecutor or by the Registry. Take a look at those. Take your time and go through them. In the Bosnian copy, the statement I am asking you about is on page 3, by the way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Does it not say: "The next day an unknown guard called Zjelko out of the hangar. I believe he was shot dead but today I cannot say for sure that I heard any shot after Klimenta was taken out." That's what it says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Which was it, sir? Did you hear a shot or didn't you hear a shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I know you either did or didn't hear a shot. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say again 100 per cent that I heard the shot, but I saw Klimenta dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So when you testified here earlier under oath that you heard a shot or a shot -- that was not true, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try it again. We all agreed a few minutes ago that you testified here under oath that you heard a shot and now you testify -- when you testified to that, that was not true, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was true. I was frightened. I didn't have freedom over there. My brain couldn't function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you could excuse me just a second, sir. Your brain could function when you met with the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor back on February 21st 1996, couldn't it? They didn't threaten you, did they? They didn't keep you in custody, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I still have problems as a result of my imprisonment. Even today my brain is not okay. After all those beatings and mistreatment and the suffering I am still not well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, because of the suffering and this treatment, do you have a problem telling what actually happened and what actually didn't happen, remembering what occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I have problems, because this was a long time ago. This was in 1992 and it's 1997 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, now let's -- okay. Let's try this again. A few minutes ago you testified that you heard a shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you have made the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I will go on to something else. If I have made my point, no reason to continue beating on it. After the shooting there was a guard, and I believe his name was Padalovic. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He came running in the hangar right after Mr. Klimenta was shot, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not Padalovic, but a prisoner Garo Kujundzic entered the hangar holding his head with his arms. We asked him "Garo, what happened?" He said Zeljko Klimenta was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, I thought we had agreed you would listen to my questions and then answer the questions. Now, if I was wrong on that agreement, can we have that agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Repeat the question so that it will be fresh in his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Did a guard named Padalovic come into the hangar shortly after the shot that you didn't hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't come into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. You testified on direct examination that Mr. Delic was the deputy commander of the camp, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's because you saw the written order appointing him deputy commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You saw some sort of a table of organisation showing what everybody's job was in the camp; is that how you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You saw a table of organisation of all the people in the camp, where everybody was slotted into a job; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't see a table of organisation of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So basically you are just guessing that Mr. Delic was the deputy commander of the camp; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not guessing. It was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you testified on direct that the entire time in the camp you saw him five or six times; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is what you said. So you didn't see him every day during your detention in Celebici, did you? I mean, you were in Celebici, what, almost six months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six months, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
